S000002Discrete topology on ω\omegaExample

Let X=ω={0,1,2,… }X=\omega=\{0,1,2,\dots\}, a set with a countably infinite number of points, and let all subsets of XX be open.

Defined as counterexample #2 ("Countable Discrete Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology.

This space is metrizable, with the standard metric for a discrete space given by d(x,y)=1d(x,y)=1 for x≠yx\ne y. A different metric that generates the same topology for XX is the Sierpiński metric (d(x,y)=1+1/(x+y+2)d(x,y)=1+1/(x+y+2) for x≠yx\ne y in ω\omega) given in counterexample #135 in Counterexamples in Topology. Since pi-base is meant to model topological properties and not properties of metrics, it only keeps track of topological spaces up to homeomorphism, and thus does not keep a separate entry for the Sierpiński metric.

S000005Odd-Even TopologyExample

Define a topology on X=ℕX = \mathbb{N} by taking as a basis all pairs {2k−1,2k}\{2k-1,2k\} for k∈ℕk \in \mathbb{N}. (Here we assume 0∉ℕ0\notin\mathbb{N}.)

Homeomorphic to the product of Discrete topology on ω\omega and Indiscrete topology on {0,1}\{0,1\}.

Defined as counterexample #6 ("Odd-Even Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology.

S000012Excluded Point Topology on a Countably Infinite SetExample

Let X=ω={0,1,2,… }X=\omega=\{0,1,2,\dots\}. A set is closed in this topology if it contains 00 or is empty.

Defined as counterexample #14 ("Countable Particular Point Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology.

<!-- [[Proof of Topology]] To prove the first condition, note that X∈τX\in \tau by definition. Now, note that ∅⊂X\emptyset \subset X and p∉∅p\notin \emptyset. It follows that ∅∈τ\emptyset \in \tau. Now to prove the second condition, consider ⋃i∈IUi\bigcup_{i\in I} U_i where II is some arbitrary indexing set. It follows that there are two cases, either p∈⋃i∈IUip\in \bigcup_{i\in I} U_i or p∉⋃i∈IUip\notin \bigcup_{i\in I} U_i. For the case in which pp is in the union, it must be the case that XX is in the union, because the only open set containing pp is XX. It follows then that the union is XX. So in this case, the second condition holds. To prove the second case, when pp is not in the union, we simply have an arbitrary union of subsets of XX which must be a subset of XX that does not contain pp. So, the second condition holds for this case. To prove the final condition, consider ⋂inUi\bigcap_i^n U_i. Again, there are two cases here, either pp is in the intersection, or it is not. For when pp is in the intersection, note that every open set other than XX does not contain pp. So for pp to be in the intersection, it must be the case that XX is the only set in the intersection and thus it is open. Now if pp is not in the intersection, it must be a subset of XX that does not contain pp. So in both cases, the intersection is open, and thus the final condition holds and τ\tau is a topology on XX. -->

S000014Either-Or TopologyExample

Let X=[−1,1]X = [-1,1] as a set and declare U⊂XU \subset X open if and only if 0∉U0 \not\in U or (−1,1)⊂U(-1,1) \subset U.

The space is homeomorphic to the topological sum of Excluded point topology on ℝ\mathbb R and Discrete topology on {0,1}\{0,1\}. (The sets {−1}\{-1\}, {1}\{1\}, (−1,1)(-1,1) form a partition of XX into clopen sets. And the subspace topology on the interval (−1,1)(-1,1) is an "excluded point topology" on a set of cardinality 𝔠\mathfrak c.)

Defined as counterexample #17 ("Either-Or Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology.

S000015Cofinite topology on ω\omegaExample

The finite complement topology on a space XX is defined by taking U⊂XU \subset X to be open if and only if X∖UX \setminus U is finite or U=∅U = \emptyset. In this case we let X=ω={0,1,2,… }X=\omega=\{0,1,2,\dots\}.

S000020Fort space on a countably infinite setExample

S000021Weak topology on separable Hilbert spaceExample

Let HH be an infinite-dimensional separable real Hilbert space (such as the space l2l^2 of square-summable sequences) with inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle. (All such spaces are isometrically isomorphic.) The continuous dual H∗H^* is the set of all linear functionals f:H→ℝf : H \to \mathbb{R} that are continuous with respect to the topology generated by the inner product. By the Riesz representation theorem, every such functional ff is of the form f(x)=⟨x,y⟩f(x) = \langle x, y \rangle for some y∈Hy \in H.

The weak topology on the set HH is the coarsest topology such that every element of H∗H^* is continuous. That is, a basis for this topology at x∈Hx \in H is the collection of all sets of the form {y∈H:∣⟨y−x,xi⟩∣<ϵ,i=1,…,n}\{ y \in H : |\langle y -x , x_i\rangle| < \epsilon, i = 1, \dots, n \} for some x1,…,xn∈Hx_1, \dots, x_n \in H and some ϵ>0\epsilon > 0.

See Definition 5.1.1 of Functional Analysis or 28.16 of Handbook of Analysis and Its Foundations. Note that the weak topology on HH is homeomorphic to the weak-* topology on H∗H^*.

Sources cited by Pi-Base

  • Functional Analysis

So 00 and xx are separated by disjoint open sets. It follows, since we are in a topological vector space, that any two points x,yx,y are separated by disjoint open sets.

Since HH is a topological vector space, the same is true for every closed ball.

    Let KnK_n be the closed ball centered at origin with radius nn, then KnK_n is compact and H=⋃n∈ωKnH = \bigcup_{n \in \omega} K_n. Suppose KK is any (weakly) compact subset of HH. From the fact that the continuous image of a compact set is compact, we know that KK is bounded in the weak topology, that is, sup⁡y∈K∣<x,y>∣<+∞\sup_{y \in K} \left| \left< x, y \right> \right| < + \infty for any x∈Hx \in H.

    Therefore, KK is bounded in norm by Uniform Boundedness Principle, thus contained in some KnK_n.

S000022Fortissimo space on ℝ\mathbb RExample

Let X=ℝX=\mathbb R and let pp be a distinguished point of XX. Every point not equal to pp is isolated and the open neighborhoods of pp are the cocountable subsets of XX containing that point.

This space is the one-point Lindelöfication of an uncountable discrete space.

Compare with Fortissimo space of size ℵ1\aleph_1 and Fortissimo space of size ℵ2\aleph_2. With a suitable assumption on ∣ℝ∣|\mathbb R| so that the cardinalities match, XX will be homeomorphic to one of them.

Defined as counterexample #25 ("Fortissimo Space") in Counterexamples in Topology.

S000027Rational numbers ℚ\mathbb QExample

Let X=ℚX=\mathbb Q, the set of rational numbers, with the subspace topology induced from Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R.

Defined as counterexample #30 ("The Rational Numbers") in Counterexamples in Topology.

A purely topological characterization of the space ℚ\mathbb Q, due to Sierpinski, is given by the following equivalent theorems:

  • Every countably infinite, Metrizable space without isolated point is homeomorphic to ℚ\mathbb Q.
  • Every countably infinite, T3T_3, First countable space without isolated point is homeomorphic to ℚ\mathbb Q.

For a proof, see Countable metric spaces without isolated points (A. Dasgupta) or Two topological uniqueness theorems for spaces of real numbers (M. Francis). And for the equivalence between the two theorems, the second one easily follows from the first; and the reverse direction follows from (Countable ∧ First countable) ⇒ Second countable together with Urysohn's metrization theorem.

It follows for example that the following spaces are homeomorphic to ℚ\mathbb Q.

(1) The space ℤ\mathbb{Z} with the Furstenberg topology, generated by all sets of the form a+kℤ={a+kn:n∈ℤ}a + k \mathbb{Z} = \{a+kn : n\in\mathbb{Z}\} with a∈ℤa\in\mathbb Z and positive integer kk.

Defined as counterexample #58 ("Evenly Spaced Integer Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology.

(2) The space ℤ\mathbb{Z} with the topology generated by all sets of the form a+pαℤ={a+pαn:n∈ℤ}a+p^\alpha\mathbb Z=\{a+p^\alpha n:n\in\mathbb Z\} with a∈ℤa\in\mathbb Z and non-negative integer α\alpha. Here pp is a fixed prime.

Defined as counterexample #59 ("The pp-adic Topology on ℤ\mathbb{Z}") in Counterexamples in Topology.

(3) The product space ℚ×ℚ\mathbb Q \times \mathbb Q.

(4) The Sorgenfrey topology on ℚ\mathbb Q, generated by all half-open intervals [p,q)∩ℚ[p,q)\cap\mathbb Q with p,q∈ℚp,q\in\mathbb Q.

S000028Irrational numbers ℝ∖ℚ\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb QExample

Let X=ℝ∖ℚX=\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q with the subspace topology from Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R.

S000030Countable product of reals ℝω\mathbb R^\omegaExample

The countable product of copies of Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R.

This space is homeomorphic to the space ℓ2\ell^2 of all sequences x=⟨xi⟩x = \langle x_i \rangle of real numbers such that ∑ixi2\sum_i x_i^2 converges, with topology generated by the metric d(x,y)=∑i(xi−yi)2d(x,y) = \sqrt{\sum_i (x_i - y_i)^2}. For this deep result due to R. D. Anderson, see for example A complete elementary proof that Hilbert space is homeomorphic to the countable infinite product of lines (Anderson & Bing). Note also that any separable Hilbert space is isomorphic to ℓ2\ell^2.

More generally, any infinite-dimensional separable Banach space or, even more generally, any infinite-dimensional separable Fréchet space is homeomorphic to ℝω\mathbb R^\omega. This is stated in Theorem VI.5.2 (Anderson-Kadec) on page 189 of Selected topics in infinite-dimensional topology (Bessaga & Pełczyński). See also wikipedia Anderson–Kadec theorem.

In particular, the following are all homeomorphic as topological spaces:

  • ℝω\mathbb R^\omega
  • Sequence spaces ℓp\ell^p (1≤p<+∞1 \leq p < + \infty)
  • Spaces Lp([0,1])L^p([0,1]) (1≤p<+∞1 \leq p < + \infty) of Lebesgue measurable functions with finite LpL^p-norm
  • The Banach space C([0,1])C([0,1]) of real-valued continuous functions on [0,1][0,1] with the supremum norm

Moreover, by Theorem VI.2.1, Corollary VI.2.2, and Theorem VI.5.1 of Selected topics in infinite-dimensional topology (Bessaga & Pełczyński) and Corollary 9.3 of A complete elementary proof that Hilbert space is homeomorphic to the countable infinite product of lines (Anderson & Bing), the following are also homeomorphic to ℝω\mathbb R^\omega:

  • The closed upper half-space of ℓ2\ell^2, i.e., {⟨xi⟩∈ℓ2:x1≥0}\{\langle x_i \rangle \in \ell^2: x_1 \geq 0\}, given the subspace topology
  • The subspace of ℓ2\ell^2 consisting of all elements with infinitely many nonzero entries, i.e., {⟨xi⟩∈ℓ2:xi≠0 for infinitely many i}\{\langle x_i \rangle \in \ell^2: x_i \neq 0 \text{ for infinitely many } i\}, given the subspace topology
  • The cone over ℝω\mathbb R^\omega, i.e., the quotient of ℝω×[0,1]\mathbb R^\omega \times [0, 1] with ℝω×{0}\mathbb R^\omega \times \{0\} identified to a single point
  • The open cone over ℝω\mathbb R^\omega, i.e., the quotient of ℝω×[0,∞)\mathbb R^\omega \times [0, \infty) with ℝω×{0}\mathbb R^\omega \times \{0\} identified to a single point
  • The unit sphere of any infinite-dimensional separable Banach space, i.e., {x∈E:∥x∥=1}\{x \in E: \|x\| = 1\} where EE is an infinite-dimensional separable Banach space under the norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|, given the topology generated by the metric d(x,y)=∥x−y∥d(x,y) = \|x-y\|; in particular, the unit sphere of ℓ2\ell^2
  • The closed unit ball of any infinite-dimensional separable Banach space, i.e., {x∈E:∥x∥≤1}\{x \in E: \|x\| \leq 1\} where EE is an infinite-dimensional separable Banach space under the norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|, given the topology generated by the metric d(x,y)=∥x−y∥d(x,y) = \|x-y\|; in particular, the closed unit ball of ℓ2\ell^2

Specific instances of the above are counterexamples #36 ("Hilbert Space"), #37 ("Fréchet Space"), and #108 ("C[0,1]C[0,1]") in Counterexamples in Topology.

S000037ω1+1\omega_1+1 with endpoint doubledExample

Let ω1\omega_1 be the first uncountable ordinal. Take ω1+1=[0,ω1]\omega_1+1=[0,\omega_1] with its usual order topology and then split the maximum point into two points, similar to the construction of Telophase topology. In other words, take X=[0,ω1]∪{ω1′}X=[0,\omega_1]\cup\{\omega'_1\} where sets of the form (β,ω1)∪{ω1′}(\beta,\omega_1)\cup\{\omega'_1\} with β<ω1\beta<\omega_1 form a neighborhood basis at ω1′\omega'_1.

See Example 1 in Answer to "Relationship between weak Hausdorff and US properties".

Explicit traits supplied by Pi-Base; omitted traits have no assertion in this record.

  • Sequentially compact
    Trait evidence · P000020

    If a sequence of elements of XX contains the same value infinitely many times, it has a convergent subsequence. Otherwise, the sequence will have a subsequence with values all in [0,ω1)[0,\omega_1). That subsequence will in turn have a convergent subsequence since Ordinal space ω1\omega_1 is Sequentially compact.

    Trait evidence · P000051

    The reasoning is similar to showing Ordinal space ω1+1\omega_1+1 is Scattered. Let AA be a nonempty subset of XX. If AA contains an element different from ω1\omega_1 and ω1′\omega'_1, the minimum element of AA is isolated in AA. Otherwise, AA is a subspace of {ω1,ω1′}\{\omega_1,\omega'_1\}, which has the discrete topology, and every element of AA is isolated in AA.

S000047Countable sum of Sierpinski spacesExample

Let XX be the set of positive integers and define a topology by declaring U⊆XU \subseteq X to be open if for every odd p∈Up \in U, p+1∈Up+1 \in U. Equivalently, A⊆XA \subseteq X is closed iff for every even p∈Ap \in A, p−1∈Ap-1 \in A.

This space is a topological sum of countably-many copies of the Sierpinski space.

Defined as counterexample #55 ("Hjalmar Ekdal Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology.

A piece of trivia: the origin of the name Hjalmar Ekdal is explained here.

<!-- [[Proof of Topology]]

  1. Note that XX contains all positive integers thus every integer pp is in XX thus XX is open. See that ∅\emptyset contains no integers therefore ∅\emptyset satisfies the condition vacuously therefore it is open.

  2. Let {Ui∣i∈I}\left\{U_i | i \in I \right\} be an arbitrary collection of open sets. Consider any odd p∈⋃i∈IUip \in \bigcup\limits_{i \in I} U_i since every UiU_i is open this means p+1p+1 is also in the union therefore the union is open.

  3. Given any intersection ⋂n=1NUn\bigcap\limits_{n=1}^N U_n with UnU_n an open set and N∈ℕN \in \mathbb{N}. Given an odd p∈⋂n=1NUnp \in \bigcap\limits_{n=1}^N U_n then p∈Unp \in U_n for all n≤Nn \leq N. Thus by definition of open p+1p+1 also exists in UnU_n for all n≤Nn \leq N therefore p+1∈⋂n=1NUnp+1 \in \bigcap\limits_{n=1}^N U_n thus ⋂n=1NUn\bigcap\limits_{n=1}^N U_n is open. -->

S000048Cofinite topology on ω\omega extended by a non-open generic pointExample

Let X=ω⊔{p}X = \omega \sqcup \{p\}. A nonempty set is open if and only if it contains pp and has a finite complement. Hence the subspace ω⊆X\omega \subseteq X equals Cofinite topology on ω\omega. Note that pp is a generic point of XX and {p}\{p\} is not open; see Has a generic point.

XX is homeomorphic to the set of prime ideals of the ring ℤ\mathbb{Z} with basis consisting of the sets Vx={P∈X:x∉P}V_x = \{P \in X : x \notin P\} for all x∈ℤ≥0x \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}. The zero ideal identifies with the generic point p∈Xp \in X. This is the Zariski topology on Spec(ℤ)\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z}), the prime spectrum of the ring of integers. See Zariski topology for the general construction of the Zariski topology on the prime spectrum of a commutative ring.

Appears as counterexample #56 ("Prime Ideal Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology.

S000049Divisor topologyExample

Let X={x∈ℕ:x≥2}X = \{x \in \mathbb{N} : x \geq 2\} with topology generated by all Un={x∈X:xU_n = \{x \in X : x divides n}n\} for n∈Xn \in X.

Defined as counterexample #57 ("Divisor Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology.

<!-- [[Proof of Topology]] To prove the set ℬ={Bn:n∈X}\mathscr{B}=\{B_n : n\in X\} is a basis for a topology on XX, we must prove:

 For every x∈X there exists some Bn such that x∈Bn\text{ For every } x\in X \text{ there exists some } B_n \text{ such that } x\in B_n  If x∈Ba∩Bb, there exists some Bc such that x∈Bc⊂Ba∩Bb\text{ If }x\in B_a \cap B_b, \text{ there exists some } B_c \text{ such that } x\in B_c\subset B_a\cap B_b

To prove the first condition, note that for every x∈Xx\in X, xx divides xx. So by definition, x∈Bxx \in B_x. To prove the second, let x∈Ba∩Bbx\in B_a\cap B_b. It follows that x∈Bax\in B_a and x∈Bbx\in B_b This is to say, xx is a common divisor of aa and bb. Note that if x∈Bnx \in B_n, it follows that xx divides nn. Therefore, all of the divisors of xx divide nn and thus are in BnB_n. The set BxB_x is the set of all divisors of xx, so x∈Bx⊂Ba∩Bbx\in B_x \subset B_a\cap B_b. We have shown that both conditions hold, so therefore the set ℬ\mathscr{B} is a basis for topology on XX. -->

Since the preimage of an open set by a continuous function is open, $$f^{-1}(\mathbb{Q} \setminus {f(f(\infty))}) = { x \mid f(x) \in \mathbb{Q} \setminus {f(f(\infty))} }$$ is an open set, containing ∞\infty but not containing f(∞)f(\infty), contradicting the fact that the only open set containing ∞\infty is XX.

S000051Khalimsky lineExample

The integers ℤ\mathbb Z with {{2i−1,2i,2i+1}∣i∈ℤ}∪{{2i+1}∣i∈ℤ}\{\{2i-1,2i,2i+1\}\mid i\in\mathbb Z\}\cup\{\{2i+1\}\mid i\in\mathbb Z\} as a basis for the topology.

This space is homeomorphic to:

  • The quotient of Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R identifying the open interval (i,i+1)(i, i + 1) to a point for each i∈ℤi \in \mathbb Z.

It is the unique Cut point space such that no proper subspace is also a cut point space. See Theorem 4.5 of Cut-point spaces (Honari & Bahrampour) for a proof.

Also named the digital line in the subject of digital topology, e.g. in On Generalized Digital Lines (Nakaoka, Tamari, Maki).

    Define a continuous map G ⁣:ℝ×I→ℝG \colon \mathbb R \times I \to \mathbb R with [ G(x, t) = \operatorname{sgn} x \cdot \min\left{ \left|x\right|, \frac t {1 - t} \right}, ] then p∘Gp \circ G is a continuous map from ℝ×I→K\mathbb R \times I \to K.

    Moreover, we have [ p(x) = p(y) \implies p \bigl( G(x, t) \bigr) = p \bigl( G(y, t) \bigr), \quad \forall x, y \in \mathbb R, \forall t \in I, ] this induces a map F ⁣:K×I→KF \colon K \times I \to K such that F(p(x),t)=p(G(x,t))F(p(x), t) = p \bigl( G(x, t) \bigr).

    Actually FF gives a homotopy from KK to {0}\{0\} since F(x,1)=xF(x, 1) = x and F(x,0)=0F(x, 0) = 0. Therefore, KK is Contractible.

S000052Relatively prime integer topologyExample

Let X=ℤ+X=\mathbb{Z}^+, the set of positive integers. For a,b∈Xa,b \in X, let Ua(b)={b+na∈X:n∈ℤ}=(b+aℤ)∩XU_a(b) = \{b+na \in X : n \in \mathbb{Z}\} = (b+a\mathbb{Z})\cap X. Then {Ua(b):a,b∈X,gcd⁡(a,b)=1}\{U_a(b) : a,b \in X, \gcd(a,b)=1\} forms a basis for the relatively prime integer topology on XX.

Alternatively, a basis is given by {Ua′(b):a,b∈X,gcd⁡(a,b)=1}\{U'_a(b) : a,b \in X, \gcd(a,b)=1\} with Ua′(b)={b+na∈X:n≥0}U'_a(b) = \{b+na \in X : n\ge 0\}. See The Kirch topology is the same as the prime integer topology for a proof of the equivalence.

As a space, XX is often called the Golomb space, for example in On continuous self-maps and homeomorphisms of the Golomb space (T. Banakh et al.). Defined as counterexample #60 ("Relatively Prime Integer Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology.

Compare with Prime integer topology, which has a coarser topology.

S000053Prime integer topologyExample

The prime integer topology on the set X=ℤ+X = \mathbb{Z}^+ of positive integers is generated by the subbasis of all sets of the form Up(b)={b+np∈X:n∈ℤ}U_p(b) = \{b+np \in X : n \in \mathbb{Z}\} for all pp prime and bb not divisible by pp. A base for the topology is given by the collection of all Ua(b)={b+na∈X:n∈ℤ}U_a(b) = \{b+na \in X : n \in \mathbb{Z}\} with a,b>0a,b>0 and with aa squarefree and relatively prime to bb.

Alternatively, a base for the topology is given by {Ua′(b):a,b∈X,gcd⁡(a,b)=1,b squarefree}\{U'_a(b) : a,b \in X, \gcd(a,b)=1, b\text{ squarefree}\} with Ua′(b)={b+na∈X:n≥0}U'_a(b) = \{b+na \in X : n\ge 0\}. See The Kirch topology is the same as the prime integer topology for a proof of the equivalence.

As a space, XX is often called the Kirch space (see references in Arithmetic progression topologies on Wikipedia). Defined as counterexample #61 ("Prime Integer Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology.

Compare with Relatively prime integer topology, which has a finer topology.

S000054Double pointed realsExample

The double pointed reals is the product XX of Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R and Indiscrete topology on {0,1}\{0,1\}.

Defined as counterexample #62 ("Double Pointed Reals") in Counterexamples in Topology.

<!-- [[Proof of Topology]] A basis for topology on ℝ×{0,1}\mathbb{R}\times \{0,1\} is generated by crossing basic open sets of ℝ\mathbb{R} with basic open sets of {0,1}\{0,1\}. The basis for the standard topology on ℝ\mathbb{R} is defined by the set ℛ={(a,b):a,b∈ℝ and a<b}\mathscr{R}=\{(a,b) : a,b\in \mathbb{R} \text{ and }a<b\}, where (a,b)(a,b) is an interval. So, the basis for topology on the Double Pointed Reals is defined by the set ℬ={A×{0,1}:A∈ℛ}\mathscr{B}=\{A\times \{0,1\}:A\in \mathscr{R}\}. More simply, ℬ={(c,d):c∈ℛ,d∈{0,1}\mathscr{B}=\{(c,d) : c\in\mathscr{R},d\in\{0,1\}, where (c,d)(c,d) is an ordered pair. In a sense, the Double Pointed Reals Topology is like keeping parallel copies of the standard topology on ℝ\mathbb{R}; one mapped to 0 and one mapped to 1. To prove the set ℬ\mathscr{B} is a basis for a topology on ℝ×{0,1}\mathbb{R}\times\{0,1\}, we must prove

 For every x∈X there exists some Bn such that x∈Bn\text{ For every } x\in X \text{ there exists some } B_n \text{ such that } x\in B_n  If x∈Ba∩Bb, there exists some Bc such that x∈Bc⊂Ba∩Bb\text{ If }x\in B_a \cap B_b, \text{ there exists some } B_c \text{ such that } x\in B_c\subset B_a\cap B_b

So to prove the first condition, let x∈ℝ×{0,1}x\in \mathbb{R}\times \{0,1\}. This implies xx is of the form (x,0) or (x,1)(x,0) \text{ or } (x,1). Suppose xx is of the form (x,0)(x,0). Let AA be some interval (a,b)(a,b) that contains xx. It is obvious that xx belongs to the ordered pair (A,0)(A,0). A similar argument follows for the case when xx is of the form (x,1)(x,1). To prove the second condition, let x∈B1∩B2x\in B_1\cap B_2. This implies B1 and B2B_1 \text{ and } B_2 have the same component of the set {0,1}\{0,1\}. Furthermore, the first element in the ordered pair of B1B_1 and B2B_2 are both of the form (a,b)(a,b) and (c,d)(c,d) respectively such that x∈(a,b) and (c,d)x\in (a,b) \text{ and } (c,d). Construct a new interval of the form, (max(a,c),min(b,d))(\text{max}(a,c),\text{min}(b,d)). It follows that xx is in this interval, and xx is in the basic open set B3B_3 with the first element as (max(a,c),min(b,d))(\text{max}(a,c),\text{min}(b,d)) and the second element the same as B1B_1 and B2B_2. Both 1 and 2 hold, so the Double Pointed Reals is a basis topology. -->

  • Lindelöf
    Trait evidence · P000018

    XX is Lindelöf: let {Ui,i∈I}\left\{U_i, i \in I\right\} be a basic open cover of XX. There are two cases:

    1: One of the UiU_i has countable complement, then we only need countably many extra UjU_j to cover all of XX, and so we find a countable subcover, or

    2: All UiU_i are standard Euclidean open sets. But then we can use that ℝ\mathbb{R} in the usual topology is Lindelöf (as it's second countable e.g.) to see that we again have a countable subcover.

    So the countable complement extension topology is Lindelöf.

  • Cozero complemented
    Trait evidence · P000061

    In order to find the Tychonoff reflection of XX, we first determine the completely regular reflection of XX, with topology generated by the cozero sets of XX.

    Note that each cozero set in a topological space is a union of regular open sets. In the current space XX, a regular open set containing a point x∈Xx\in X also contains a Euclidean neighborhood of xx. For the non-obvious case of x=0x=0, it is because int⁡XclX((−ε,ε)∖K)=int⁡X[−ε,ε]=(−ε,ε)\operatorname{int}_X\text{cl}_X((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\setminus K) = \operatorname{int}_X[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon] = (-\varepsilon,\varepsilon). So the topology generated by the cozero sets of XX is contained in the Euclidean topology of ℝ\mathbb R. On the other hand, Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R · Completely regular. So the completely regular reflection of XX is Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R. And since ℝ\mathbb R is even Tychonoff, it is the Tychonoff reflection of XX.

    The reflection map φ\varphi is the identity function on ℝ\mathbb R as a set; it is open at each point xx of the dense subset X∖{0}⊆XX\setminus\{0\}\subseteq X (i.e., sends neighborhoods of xx to neighborhoods of f(x)f(x)). Since Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R · Cozero complemented, the desired result then follows from the Remark after Proposition 2 in Cozero complemented property for a space and its Tychonoff reflection.

S000057Rational sequence topologyExample

S000063Michael lineExample

Let D=ℝ∖ℚD=\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q, the set of irrational numbers. The space XX is ℝ\mathbb R with the topology generated by the Euclidean open sets together with all singletons {x}\{x\} for x∈Dx\in D. (So any subset of DD is open in XX.)

The topology is finer than Indiscrete irrational extension of ℝ\mathbb R.

The use of this space by Ernest Michael in The product of a normal space and a metric space need not be normal (E. Michael) resulted in it being known as the "Michael line". See for example https://dantopology.wordpress.com/2012/10/28/michael-line-basics/.

Defined as counterexample #71 ("Discrete Irrational Extension of ℝ\mathbb{R}") in Counterexamples in Topology.

    Let {qn:n∈ℕ}=ℚ\{q_n: n\in\mathbb N\}=\mathbb Q. Consider the set L=ℝ∖⋃n∈ℕ(qn−2−n,qn+2−n)L = \mathbb R\setminus \bigcup_{n\in \mathbb N} (q_n-2^{-n},q_n+2^{-n}), which is closed in Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R and hence closed in the finer topology of XX. S000064Rational extension of the planeExample

S000067Irrational slope topologyExample

Let X={(x,y):x,y∈ℚ,y≥0}X = \{(x,y) : x,y \in \mathbb{Q}, y \geq 0\}. For a fixed irrational θ>0\theta>0, the irrational slope topology on XX is obtained by taking as a local base of open neighborhoods of each point (x,y)∈X(x,y)\in X the collection of sets Nϵ(x,y)N_\epsilon(x,y) with ϵ>0\epsilon>0, defined by Nϵ(x,y)={(x,y)}∪B(x−y/θ,ϵ)∪B(x+y/θ,ϵ)N_\epsilon(x,y) = \{(x,y)\} \cup B(x - y/\theta, \epsilon) \cup B(x + y/\theta, \epsilon) where B(a,ϵ):=((a−ϵ,a+ϵ)∩ℚ)×{0}B(a, \epsilon):=((a-\epsilon,a+\epsilon)\cap\mathbb Q)\times\{0\}. That is, Nϵ(x,y)N_\epsilon(x,y) consists of the point (x,y)(x,y) together with the rational numbers in an ϵ\epsilon-neighborhood around the two points where the lines passing through (x,y)(x,y) with slopes θ\theta and −θ-\theta cross the real xx-axis.

Defined as counterexample #75 ("Irrational Slope Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology. Originally introduced in A connected countable Hausdorff space (R.H. Bing) with θ=3\theta=\sqrt 3.

  • ¬Countably-many continuous self-maps
    Trait evidence · P000138

    Following the terminology used in The connected countable spaces of Bing and Ritter are topologically homogeneous (Banakh et al.), a set A⊂XA\subset X is called θ\theta-discrete if every point of XX has a closed neighbourhood containing only one point of AA. (The symbol "θ\theta" here has nothing to do with the irrational constant used to define Irrational slope topology.)

    By Theorem 1 in that paper, every bijection between θ\theta-discrete subsets of XX extends to a homeomorphism from XX to itself.

    The set ℤ×{0}\mathbb Z\times\{0\} is θ\theta-discrete (every discrete closed subset contained in ℚ×{0}\mathbb Q\times\{0\} is) and admits continuum many bijections to itself (e.g. every subset of ZZ with at least two elements in its complement can be the set of fixed points). Hence there exist uncountably many self-homeomorphisms of XX.

S000068Deleted diameter topologyExample

Let X=ℝ2X = \mathbb{R}^2. The deleted diameter topology on XX is generated by the basis consisting of all open discs with their horizontal diameters except the center deleted.

Defined as counterexample #76 ("Deleted Diameter Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology. (That reference states that the deleted discs above form a subbasis for the topology, but they in fact form a basis.)

    Moreover, inteAn=∅\mathrm{int}_e A_n=\emptyset, since a Euclidean ball centred at x∈Anx\in A_n contains elements of inteU\mathrm{int}_e U for any UU with x∈U∈𝒰nx\in U\in\mathscr U_n. Therefore the AnA_n are nowhere dense subsets of the Euclidean plane.

S000070Half-disc topologyExample

Let H={(x,y)∈ℝ2:y>0}H = \{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : y>0\} be the upper half plane and LL the xx-axis. The half disc topology on X=H∪LX = H \cup L is the topology generated by the following neighborhood bases: points x∈Hx\in H have the usual Euclidean neighborhoods and points x∈Lx \in L have neighborhoods of the form {x}∪(H∩U)\{x\} \cup (H \cap U) where x∈Ux \in U and UU is open in the usual Euclidean topology.

Defined as counterexample #78 ("Half-Disc Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology.

An order on the neighbourhood V1V_1 of ⟨0,0⟩\langle 0,0\rangle can be defined using the injective map s(⟨i,k⟩):=⟨min⁡{i,k},i−k⟩∈ℕ×ℤs(\langle i,k\rangle ):= \langle\min\{i,k\},i-k\rangle \in\mathbb N\times\mathbb Z. Declare ⟨0,0⟩\langle 0,0\rangle to be the maximal element, and for p,q∈V1∩Ap,q\in V_1\cap A define p≤qp\leq q iff s(p)≤lexs(q)s(p)\leq_{lex}s(q). Given such order on V1V_1:

    1. Each point in V1∩AV_1\cap A has a successor and a predecessor, hence is isolated in the order topology.
    2. A base neighbourhood of ⟨0,0⟩\langle 0,0\rangle in the original topology is Vn=⋃k≥0(⟨n,n+k⟩,→)V_n=\bigcup_{k\geq 0}(\langle n,n+k\rangle,\rightarrow), which is open in the order topology. On the other hand, an order neighbourhood of ⟨0,0⟩\langle 0,0\rangle, which is of the form (⟨i,k⟩,→)(\langle i,k\rangle,\rightarrow), contains the set Vmin⁡{i,k}+1V_{\min\{i,k\}+1}, and therefore is a neighbourhood in the original topology.

    Hence the order topology coincides with the original topology on V1V_1.

S000072Arens squareExample

Let S=((0,1)ℚ∖{12})×(0,1)ℚS=\big((0,1)_{\mathbb Q}\setminus\{\frac{1}{2}\}\big)\times(0,1)_{\mathbb Q} and X=S∪{⟨0,0⟩,⟨1,0⟩}∪{⟨12,r2⟩:r∈(0,12)ℚ}X=S\cup\{\langle 0,0\rangle,\langle 1,0\rangle\}\cup\{\langle\frac{1}{2},r\sqrt{2}\rangle:r\in(0,\frac{1}{\sqrt 2})_{\mathbb Q}\} (where Iℚ=I∩ℚI_{\mathbb Q}=I\cap\mathbb Q).

This space is XX with the topology such that points of SS have their usual neighborhoods as a subspace of Euclidean Plane ℝ2\mathbb R^2, and

  • Un(0,0)={⟨0,0⟩}∪((0,14)ℚ×(0,1n)ℚ)U_n(0,0) = \{\langle 0,0\rangle\} \cup \left((0,\frac{1}{4})_{\mathbb Q}\times(0,\frac{1}{n})_{\mathbb Q}\right),
  • Un(1,0)={⟨1,0⟩}∪((34,1)ℚ×(0,1n)ℚ)U_n(1,0) = \{\langle 1,0\rangle\} \cup \left((\frac{3}{4},1)_{\mathbb Q}\times(0,\frac{1}{n})_{\mathbb Q}\right), and
  • Un(12,r2)=((14,34)×(r2−1n,r2+1n))∩XU_n(\frac{1}{2},r\sqrt{2}) = \left((\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{4})\times(r\sqrt{2}-\frac{1}{n},r\sqrt{2}+\frac{1}{n})\right)\cap X for r∈(0,12)ℚr\in(0,\frac{1}{\sqrt 2})_{\mathbb Q}.

are local bases at ⟨0,0⟩\langle 0,0\rangle, ⟨1,0⟩\langle 1,0\rangle and ⟨12,r2⟩\langle\frac{1}{2},r\sqrt{2}\rangle respectively.

Defined as counterexample #80 ("Arens Square") in Counterexamples in Topology, where this space was erroneously claimed to be T212T_{2 \frac{1}{2}}. Compare with B. Scott's modified Arens square which modifies the construction to obtain a valid T212T_{2 \frac{1}{2}} example.

S000075Rational tangent disc topologyExample

Let XX consist of the open upper half plane along with the rational points on the xx-axis. Let points in the upper half plane have their usual Euclidean neighborhoods. S000080B. Scott's modified Arens squareExample

The authors of Counterexamples in Topology intended the Arens square space (counterexample #80) to be an example of a space that is T212T_{2 \frac{1}{2}} and Semiregular, but not T3T_3 and not Functionally Hausdorff. It turns out Arens square was erroneously claimed as T212T_{2 \frac{1}{2}} in their book. Brian Scott constructed the modification below in Answer to "Is Arens Square a Urysohn space?" to provide an example with the desired properties.

Let QQ be the set of rational points in the interval (0,1)(0,1) and let {Qq:q∈Q}\{Q_q:q\in Q\} be a partition of QQ into countably many dense subsets. Let

S=⋃q∈Q({q}×Qq)S=\bigcup_{q\in Q}(\{q\}\times Q_q)

and take the space to be X={(0,0),(1,0)}∪SX=\{(0,0),(1,0)\}\cup S.

Let M={1/2}×Q1/2M=\{1/2\}\times Q_{1/2}. Points of S∖MS\setminus M have the neighborhoods that they inherit from the Euclidean topology. Local bases at the points (0,0)(0,0), (1,0)(1,0) and (1/2,q)∈M(1/2,q)\in M are given respectively by the collections of sets

  • Un(0,0)={(0,0)}∪{(x,y)∈S:0<x<14,  0<y<1n}U_n(0,0) = \{(0,0)\} \cup \{(x,y)\in S: 0<x<\frac14, \; 0<y<\frac1n\},
  • Un(1,0)={(1,0)}∪{(x,y)∈S:34<x<1,  0<y<1n}U_n(1,0) = \{(1,0)\} \cup \{(x,y)\in S: \frac34<x<1, \; 0<y<\frac1n\},
  • Un(1/2,q)={(x,y)∈S:14<x<34,  q−1n<y<q+1n}.U_n(1/2,q) = \{(x,y)\in S: \frac{1}{4}<x<\frac34, \; q-\frac1n < y < q+\frac1n\}.

The properties and justifications given for counterexample #80 in Counterexamples in Topology are valid for this space with minimal modifications.

  • Semilocally simply connected
    Trait evidence · P000229

    The subspace topology on [0,ω1)×[−1,1]⊆X[0, \omega_1) \times [-1, 1] \subseteq X is the standard product topology. The subspace topology on {ω1}×[−1,1]⊆X\{\omega_1\} \times [-1, 1] \subseteq X is a (topological) disjoint union of {ω1}×[−1,0)\{\omega_1\} \times [-1, 0) and {ω1}×[0,1]\{\omega_1\} \times [0, 1] with their standard topologies. XX has a finer topology than [0,ω1]×[−1,1][0, \omega_1] \times [-1, 1] with the product topology.

    It follows that the path components of XX are {ω1}×[−1,0)\{\omega_1\} \times [-1, 0), {ω1}×[0,1]\{\omega_1\} \times [0, 1], and {α}×[−1,1]\{\alpha\} \times [-1, 1] for each α<ω1\alpha < \omega_1, all with their standard topologies. Thus each path component is homeomorphic to Interval [0,1)[0,1) or Unit interval [0,1][0,1].

    The result follows since Interval [0,1)[0,1) · Semilocally simply connected and Unit interval [0,1][0,1] · Semilocally simply connected.

S000083Line with two originsExample

The space XX is obtained by taking ℝ\mathbb R (Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R) and replacing the origin 00 with two origins 010_1 and 020_2. Basic open neighborhoods of a point x≠0x\ne 0 are the Euclidean open neighborhoods of xx not containing 00. Basic open neighborhoods of each origin 0i0_i are of the form (U∖{0})∪{0i}(U\setminus\{0\})\cup\{0_i\} with UU a Euclidean open neighborhood of 00.

The space can also be obtained as a quotient space of the disjoint union of ℝ×{1}\mathbb R\times\{1\} and ℝ×{2}\mathbb R\times\{2\} by identifying points (x,1)(x,1) and (x,2)(x,2) for x≠0x\ne 0.

This space is similar to Telophase topology and provides an example of a Locally nn-Euclidean space that is not T2T_2.

See Non-Hausdorff manifold on Wikipedia and Exercise 5 of section 36 in Topology (Munkres).

S000084Line with countably many originsExample

This space is similar to Line with two origins, but with a countably infinite number of origins. Given SS a countably infinite set with the discrete topology, the space can be constructed as a quotient space of ℝ×S\mathbb R \times S by identifying points (x,α)(x,\alpha) and (x,β)(x,\beta) whenever x≠0x\ne 0.

Equivalently, it can be obtained from ℝ\mathbb R by replacing the origin 00 with many origins 0α0_\alpha, one for each α∈S\alpha \in S. The subspace ℝ∖{0}\mathbb R\setminus\{0\} retains its Euclidean topology. Basic open neighborhoods of each origin 0α0_\alpha are of the form (U∖{0})∪{0α}(U\setminus \{0\})\cup \{0_\alpha\} with UU an open neighborhood of 00 in ℝ\mathbb R.

See Non-Hausdorff manifold on Wikipedia.

Equivalently, it can be obtained from ℝ\mathbb R by replacing the origin 00 with many origins 0α0_\alpha, one for each α∈S\alpha \in S. The subspace ℝ∖{0}\mathbb R\setminus\{0\} retains its Euclidean topology. Basic open neighborhoods of each origin 0α0_\alpha are of the form (U∖{0})∪{0α}(U\setminus \{0\})\cup \{0_\alpha\} with UU an open neighborhood of 00 in ℝ\mathbb R.

S000086Everywhere doubled lineExample

This space is similar to Line with two origins, with every point "doubled".

The space can be described as the union of two real lines X=A⊔BX=A\sqcup B with A=ℝ×{0}A = \mathbb R\times\{0\} and B=ℝ×{1}B=\mathbb R\times\{1\}. A set U⊆XU\subseteq X is open exactly when U∩AU\cap A is open in AA with the usual Euclidean topology and for each x=(r,1)∈U∩Bx=(r,1)\in U\cap B, the set UU contains a deleted neighborhood of (r,0)(r,0) in AA.

Equivalently, this space has the topology on X=ℝ×{0,1}X= \mathbb R\times\{0,1\} generated by the basic open sets B(⟨x,i⟩,ϵ)={⟨x,i⟩}∪(((x−ϵ,x)∪(x,x+ϵ))×{0})B(\langle x,i\rangle,\epsilon)=\{\langle x,i\rangle\}\cup\Big(\Big((x-\epsilon,x)\cup(x,x+\epsilon)\Big)\times\{0\}\Big) for each point ⟨x,i⟩∈X\langle x,i\rangle\in X and ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

See section 3 of Manifolds: Hausdorffness versus homogeneity (Baillif & Gabard) and the description of the general construction in Answer to "T1 spaces where the closure of a compact set is not compact".

This provides an example of a Locally nn-Euclidean space that is not T2T_2, but is Homogeneous.

    We can construct a GδG_\delta-diagonal sequence 𝒰1,𝒰2,…\mathscr U_1,\mathscr U_2, \dots by letting 𝒰n={B(⟨x,1⟩,1/n):x∈ℝ}\mathscr U_n=\{B(\langle x,1\rangle,1/n):x\in\mathbb R\}, where

    B(⟨x,1⟩,1n)={⟨x,1⟩}∪(((x−1n,x)∪(x,x+1n))×{0})\quad B(\langle x,1\rangle,\frac1n)=\{\langle x,1\rangle\}\cup\big(((x-\frac1n,x)\cup(x,x+\frac1n))\times\{0\}\big)

    is a basic open neighborhood around the point ⟨x,1⟩\langle x,1\rangle in the top line as described in the definition of the space.

One easily checks that for a point ⟨x,1⟩\langle x,1\rangle in the top line, st⁡(⟨x,1⟩,𝒰n)=B(⟨x,1⟩,1n)\operatorname{st}(\langle x,1\rangle,\mathscr U_n)=B(\langle x,1\rangle,\frac1n); and for a point ⟨x,0⟩\langle x,0\rangle in the bottom line, st⁡(⟨x,0⟩,𝒰n)⊆((x−2n,x+2n)×{0,1})∖{⟨x,1⟩}\operatorname{st}(\langle x,0\rangle,\mathscr U_n)\subseteq((x-\frac2n,x+\frac2n)\times\{0,1\}) \setminus\{\langle x,1\rangle\}. From there it follows that ⋂nst⁡(⟨x,i⟩,𝒰n)={⟨x,i⟩}\bigcap_n\operatorname{st}(\langle x,i\rangle,\mathscr U_n)=\{\langle x,i\rangle\} for all ⟨x,i⟩∈X\langle x,i\rangle\in X.

  • Has a σ\sigma-locally finite network
    Trait evidence · P000117

    Let ℬ\mathcal B be a countable base of the Euclidean topology on ℝ\mathbb R. As a σ\sigma-locally finite network 𝒩\mathcal N take the union of the countably many families {B×{0}}\{B{\times}\{0\} \} for B∈ℬB\in \mathcal B and {{(x,1)}:x∈ℝ}\{\{(x,1)\}: x\in \mathbb R\}. Each of these families is locally finite, as every point of XX admits a neighbourhood intersecting at most one set from each of those families.

    𝒩\mathcal N is a refinement of a base of the topology on XX, hence it is a network.

S000087Deleted Dieudonné plankExample

The subspace XX of Dieudonné plank obtained by removing the point ⟨ω1,ω⟩\langle\omega_1,\omega\rangle. So X=(Y×Z)∖{⟨ω1,ω⟩}X=(Y\times Z)\setminus\{\langle\omega_1,\omega\rangle\} where Y=[0,ω1]Y=[0,\omega_1] is given the topology with points of [0,ω1)[0,\omega_1) isolated and neighborhoods of ω1\omega_1 cocountable (Fortissimo space of size ℵ1\aleph_1), and Z=[0,ω]Z=[0,\omega] is given the topology with points of [0,ω)[0,\omega) isolated and neighborhoods of ω\omega cofinite (Fort space on a countably infinite set).

Defined as counterexample #89 ("Dieudonné Plank") in Counterexamples in Topology. Note that the pi-Base qualifies this name with "Deleted" to align with e.g. Tychonoff plank and Deleted Tychonoff plank.

Also, there have to be at most finitely many non-empty such columns (picking a single point from each column leads to a closed and discrete subset). And finally, AA has a finite intersection with {ω1}×[0,ω)\{\omega_1\}{\times}[0,\omega). It follows that AA is closed as a finite union of closed sets.

S000088Tychonoff corkscrewExample

The space X=DJ(Y,H,K)X=\mathrm{DJ}(Y,H,K) is the result of applying the double-sided variation of the "Jones machine" to the space Y=Y= Deleted Tychonoff plank and its two closed subsets H=ω1×{ω}H=\omega_1\times\{\omega\} and K={ω1}×ωK=\{\omega_1\}\times\omega (which have the property that they cannot be separated by open sets in YY). It is obtained by taking a two-sided sequence of copies of YY, plus two extra limit points a−,a+a^-, a^+, and alternately gluing adjacent copies of YY along either HH or KK.

Formally, define Z=(Y×ℤ)∪{p−,p+}Z = (Y\times \mathbb{Z}) \cup \{p^-, p^+\}, where p±p^\pm are two new points, to have topology such that U⊆ZU\subseteq Z is open iff U∩(Y×ℤ)U\cap (Y\times \mathbb{Z}) is open in the product topology where ℤ\mathbb{Z} is discrete, and if p+∈Up^+\in U (resp. p−∈Up^-\in U) then Y×{n∈ℤ:n≥N}⊆UY\times \{n\in \mathbb{Z} : n\geq N\}\subseteq U (resp. Y×{n∈ℤ:n≤−N}⊆UY\times \{n\in \mathbb{Z} : n\leq -N\}\subseteq U) for some N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}. Define X=DJ(Y,H,K)X=\mathrm{DJ}(Y,H,K) as the quotient space Z/∼Z/{\sim} where the equivalence relation ∼\sim is given by (x,2n)∼(x,2n+1)(x, 2n)\sim (x, 2n+1) for x∈Hx\in H and (x,2n−1)∼(x,2n)(x, 2n-1)\sim (x, 2n) for x∈Kx\in K, and no other relations between distinct points. If q:Z→Xq:Z\to X is the quotient map, define a±=q(p±)a^\pm = q(p^\pm).

The construction above is described in Problem 1Y in Extensions and absolutes of Hausdorff spaces, based on the original idea in Hereditarily separable, non-completely regular spaces.

The space XX is defined in a more informal way as counterexample #90 ("Tychonoff Corkscrew") in Counterexamples in Topology.

S000090Hewitt's condensed corkscrewExample

If T=DJ(Y,H,K)T = \text{DJ}(Y, H, K) is the Tychonoff corkscrew, Hewitt's condensed corkscrew is the set X=(T∖{a+,a−})×ω1X = (T\setminus \{a^+, a^-\}) \times \omega_1 with the subspace topology induced from a certain topology τA\tau_A on A=T×ω1A = T \times \omega_1 which we define below.

Let Γ:X×X→ω1\Gamma:X \times X \rightarrow \omega_1 be a fixed bijection and πi:X×X→X\pi_i:X\times X\to X be the coordinate projections. Define ψ:A∖X→X\psi: A \setminus X \rightarrow X by ψ(a+,λ)=π1(Γ−1(λ))\psi(a^+, \lambda) = \pi_1 (\Gamma^{-1}(\lambda)) and ψ(a−,λ)=π2(Γ−1(λ))\psi(a^-, \lambda) = \pi_2 (\Gamma^{-1}(\lambda)). Define Aλ=T×{λ}A_\lambda = T\times \{\lambda\} for λ∈ω1\lambda\in \omega_1 and let σλ\sigma_\lambda be the product topology on AλA_\lambda (so that (Aλ,σλ)(A_\lambda, \sigma_\lambda) and TT are homeomorphic). Then define $$\tau_A = {U\subseteq A : \psi^{-1}(U)\subseteq U \text{ and }U\cap A_\lambda\in \sigma_\lambda\text{ for all }\lambda\in\omega_1}.$$ Note that the topology τA↾Aλ\tau_A\restriction A_\lambda is coarser than σλ\sigma_\lambda, and can be strictly coarser for a given λ\lambda.

Let L0={(x,0) ∣ x∈(0,1)}L_0 = \{(x,0)\ |\ x \in (0,1)\} and for i≥1i \geq 1, Li={(x,1i)∣ x∈[0,1)}L_i = \{(x,\frac{1}{i}) |\ x \in [0,1)\}, and X=⋃i=0∞LiX = \bigcup_{i=0}^\infty L_i. If i≥1i \geq 1, each point of Li∖{(0,1i)}L_i \setminus \{(0, \frac{1}{i})\} is open. Basis neighborhoods of (0,1i)(0,\frac{1}{i}) are subsets LiL_i with finite complements. The sets Ui(x,0)={(x,0)}∪{(x,1n) ∣ n>i}U_i(x,0) = \{(x,0)\} \cup \{(x,\frac{1}{n})\ |\ n > i\} form a basis for the points in L0L_0.

This space is homeomorphic to (Y1×Y2)∖{(∞,∞)}(Y_1\times Y_2)\setminus \{(\infty, \infty)\} where $Y_1 = $Fort space on the real numbers and Y2=Y_2=Fort space on a countably infinite set.

S000092Thomas corkscrewExample

The space X=DJ(Y,H,K)X=\mathrm{DJ}(Y,H,K) is the result of applying the double-sided variation of the "Jones machine" to the space Y=Y= Thomas plank and its two closed subsets H=L0H = L_0 and K={(0,1n):n∈ℕ}K = \{(0, \frac{1}{n}) : n\in\mathbb{N}\} (which have the property that they cannot be separated by open sets in YY). It is obtained by taking a two-sided sequence of copies of YY, plus two extra limit points a−,a+a^-, a^+, and alternately gluing adjacent copies of YY along either HH or KK.

    We will prove that the Concentric Circles Topology is T2T_2 by cases. There are four cases. To show that C1C_1 is closed it is enough to show that the complement of C1C_1 is open thus we will construct the complement of C1C_1 since C1={x∈ℝ2:∣x∣=1}C_1 = \left\{x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |x| = 1 \right\} thus

S000097One-point compactification of the sequential fan SωS_\omegaExample

The set ω2∪{x,y}\omega^2\cup\{x,y\} topologized by the following basis: points of ω2\omega^2 are isolated, {x}∪{⟨i,j⟩∈ω2:i≥f(j)}\{x\}\cup\{\langle i,j\rangle\in\omega^2 : i\geq f(j)\} is open for each f:ω→ωf:\omega\to\omega, and {y}∪{⟨i,j⟩∈ω2:j≥n}\{y\}\cup\{\langle i,j\rangle\in\omega^2 : j\geq n\} is open for each n<ωn<\omega. Put another way, neighborhoods of xx contain all but finitely-many points of each row of ω2\omega^2, and neighborhoods of yy contain all but finitely-many rows.

Equivalently, this is the one-point compactification of a copy ω2∪{x}\omega^2\cup\{x\} of Sequential fan with ω\omega-many spines with yy as its compactifying point.

Defined as counterexample #99 ("Maximal Compact Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology to demonstrate an example of a non-T2T_2 space which has a maximal compact topology.

S000099Alexandroff squareExample

Let XX be the unit square [0,1]×[0,1]⊂ℝ2[0,1] \times [0,1] \subset \mathbb{R}^2. For a point (x,y)(x,y) not on the diagonal (for x≠yx \ne y), basic neighborhoods are given by the vertical segments {x}×(y−ε,y+ε)\{x\} \times (y - \varepsilon,y + \varepsilon) for ε>0\varepsilon > 0. For a point (x,x)(x,x) on the diagonal, basic open neighborhoods are given by open horizontal strips minus a finite number of vertical lines, i.e., sets of the form S×(x−ε,x+ε)S \times (x - \varepsilon,x + \varepsilon) for ε>0\varepsilon > 0 and SS cofinite subset of [0,1][0,1] containing xx.

Every vertical slice is homeomorphic to Unit interval [0,1][0,1]. Every horizontal slice is homeomorphic to Fort space on the real numbers, with the homeomorphism sending the point on the diagonal to ∞\infty. The diagonal {(x,x)∣x∈[0,1]}\{(x,x) | x \in [0, 1]\} is homeomorphic to Unit interval [0,1][0,1].

Defined as counterexample #101 ("Alexandroff Square") in Counterexamples in Topology.

S000100David Gao's ultraconnected non-contractible spaceExample

David Gao's example of a nonempty Ultraconnected space that is not Contractible, as constructed in Answer to "Are hereditarily connected spaces and ultraconnected spaces contractible?".

The underlying set is the set XX of partial functions ff from ℤ\mathbb{Z} to {0,1}\{0, 1\} satisfying all of the following three conditions:

  1. There exists n∈ℤn \in \mathbb{Z} such that the domain of ff is ℤ≤n\mathbb{Z}_{\leq n}. We call nn the length of ff, which shall be denoted by l(f)l(f).
  2. There exists n∈ℤn \in \mathbb{Z} such that f(m)=0f(m) = 0 for all m≤nm \leq n.
  3. Either range(f)={0}\text{range}(f) = \{0\} and l(f)≤0l(f) \leq 0; or there exists n<0n < 0 such that f(n)=1f(n) = 1, and furthermore if n0=min⁡{n<0:f(n)=1}n_0 = \min\{n < 0: f(n) = 1\}, then l(f)≤−n0l(f) \leq -n_0.

For partial functions f,gf, g from ℤ\mathbb{Z} to {0,1}\{0, 1\}, we shall say gg is a truncation of ff, denoted by g≤fg \leq f, if there exists n∈ℤn \in \mathbb{Z} s.t. g=f∣dom(f)∩ℤ≤ng = f|_{\text{dom}(f) \cap \mathbb{Z}_{\leq n}}. Truncations of elements of XX are also in XX. Furthermore, ≤\leq is a partial order on XX.

To define the topology on XX, for each x∈Xx \in X, let

Tx={y∈X:y≤x}.T_x = \{y \in X: y \leq x\}.

And for each n∈ℤn \in \mathbb{Z}, let

Kn={y∈X:l(y)≤n}.K_n = \{y \in X: l(y) \leq n\}.

The set XX is equipped with the topology generated by the closed subbasis

{Tx:x∈X}∪{Kn:n∈ℤ};\{T_x: x \in X\} \cup \{K_n: n \in \mathbb{Z}\};

that is, the topology on XX is generated by the subbasis of open sets consisting of the complements of the TxT_x and the complements of the KnK_n.

S000102Baire space of weight continuum B(𝔠)B(\mathfrak c)Example

XX is the product of countably many copies of Discrete topology on ℝ\mathbb R. So X=ℝωX=\mathbb R^\omega with ℝ\mathbb R having the discrete topology.

In general, the Baire space of weight κ\kappa for some infinite cardinal κ\kappa is the countable power DωD^\omega for some discrete space DD with ∣D∣=κ|D|=\kappa, and is denoted B(κ)B(\kappa). It has weight κ\kappa. The current space is X=B(𝔠)=B(2ℵ0)X=B(\mathfrak c)=B(2^{\aleph_0}).

This space is metrizable using the Baire metric. For distinct elements x=(xi)i≥0,y=(yi)i≥0x=(x_i)_{i\ge 0}, y=(y_i)_{i\ge 0} in X=DωX=D^\omega the Baire metric is defined by d(x,y)=1i+1d(x,y)=\frac{1}{i+1} where ii is the first coordinate with xi≠yix_i\neq y_i. And d(x,x)=0d(x,x)=0.

See Example 4.2.12 in General Topology (Engelking, 1989).

Also defined as counterexample #104 ("Baire Metric on ℝω\mathbb{R}^\omega") in Counterexamples in Topology, where the index starts at i=1i=1.

This space has a finer topology than Countable product of reals ℝω\mathbb R^\omega.

S000103Continuum power of [0,1][0,1]Example

The product topology on X=IIX=I^I, where II is the Unit interval [0,1][0,1]. In other words it is the set of all functions f ⁣:I→If\colon I\to I, endowed with the topology of pointwise convergence.

In general, the Tychonoff cube of weight κ\kappa for an infinite cardinal κ\kappa is the product space [0,1]κ[0,1]^\kappa, as defined on page 83 of General Topology (Engelking, 1989). It has topological weight κ\kappa (see Theorem 2.3.23 in the same reference). The current space XX is the Tychonoff cube of weight 𝔠\mathfrak c.

Defined as counterexample #105 ("III^I") in Counterexamples in Topology.

Compare with Hilbert cube [0,1]ω[0,1]^\omega, which is the Tychonoff cube of weight ℵ0\aleph_0.

S000108Stone-Čech compactification βω\beta\omega of the integersExample

The Stone-Čech compactification of Discrete topology on ω\omega. One way to describe X=βωX=\beta \omega is as the set of all ultrafilters on ω={0,1,2,… }\omega=\{0,1,2,\dots\}, where we identify n∈ωn \in \omega with the principal ultrafilter containing nn. The topology on XX is generated by all sets of the form U‾={F∈βω:U∈F}\overline U = \{F \in \beta\omega : U \in F\} for U⊆ωU \subseteq \omega.

S000109Novak spaceExample

The space XX is the subspace A1=ℕ∪PA_1 = \mathbb N\cup P of βℕ\beta\mathbb N (Stone-Čech compactification βω\beta\omega of the integers) constructed in the proof of Theorem 3 in On the Cartesian product of two compact spaces (J. Novak).

Using the alternative notation βω\beta\omega, the construction goes as follows. There are 2𝔠2^\mathfrak{c} countably infinite subsets of βω\beta\omega. Let {Sξ:ξ<λ}\{S_\xi : \xi<\lambda\} enumerate them all, where λ\lambda is the first ordinal of cardinality 2𝔠2^\mathfrak{c}. By transfinite recursion one can find elements xξ,yξ∈βω∖ωx_\xi,y_\xi\in\beta\omega\setminus\omega for all ξ\xi such that:

  1. xξ,yξ∈Sξ‾∖Sξx_\xi, y_\xi\in \overline{S_\xi}\setminus S_\xi;

  2. all the xξx_\xi are distinct and all the yξy_\xi are distinct;

  3. the sets {xξ:ξ<λ}\{x_\xi:\xi<\lambda\} and {yξ:ξ<λ}\{y_\xi:\xi<\lambda\} form a partition of βω∖ω\beta\omega\setminus\omega.

Then X=ω∪{xξ:ξ<λ}X=\omega\cup\{x_\xi:\xi<\lambda\} with the subspace topology induced from βω\beta\omega.

Defined as counterexample #112 ("Novak Space") in Counterexamples in Topology. However, the construction in that book is incorrect as it assumes that 2𝔠2^\mathfrak{c} is a regular cardinal, while it is consistent with ZFC that it isn't.

S000110Strong ultrafilter topologyExample

Let MM be the set of all free ultrafilters on ω\omega. The strong ultrafilter topology is the set X=ω∪MX = \omega \cup M with topology generated by singletons of ω\omega along with all sets of the form A∪{F}A \cup \{F\} for A∈F∈MA \in F \in M.

S000111Single ultrafilter subspace of βω\beta\omegaExample

Let FF be a non-principal ultrafilter on ω\omega. The space XX is the set ω∪{F}\omega\cup\{F\} with points of ω\omega isolated and neighborhoods of FF all sets of the form U∪{F}U \cup \{F\} for U∈FU \in F.

This is the subspace topology on ω∪{F}\omega\cup\{F\} induced as a subset of βω\beta\omega (Stone-Čech compactification βω\beta\omega of the integers).

Defined as counterexample #114 ("Single Ultrafilter Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology.

S000118Integer broomExample

Let X⊂ℝ2X \subset \mathbb{R}^2 consist of points with polar coordinates {(n,θ) ∣ n∈ω,θ∈{0}∪{1/n}n=1∞}\{(n,\theta)\ \mid\ n \in \omega, \theta \in \{0\} \cup \{1/n\}_{n=1}^\infty\}. Define a topology on XX by taking as a basis all sets of the form U×VU \times V where UU is an open set in the right order topology on the positive integers and VV is open in {0}∪{1/n}n=1∞⊂ℝ\{0\} \cup \{1/n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathbb{R}. The only neighborhood of the origin is XX itself.

This space is the quotient of the product of Right ray topology on ω\omega with Fort space on a countably infinite set where all points whose first component is 00 are identified.

    Observe that every point of XX not of the form (0,n+12,0)(0,n+\frac{1}{2},0) (endpoint of some segment BkB_k) admits a neighbourhood in XX that is closed in ℝ3\mathbb R^3 (hence Completely metrizable). Its interior in XX is then Completely metrizable as well.

    Therefore Player 1 cannot pick xnx_n of this form, because the next move of Player 2 would reduce the game to the case of a completely metrizable space VnV_n, which is Strongly Choquet (Explore). (Let us call this the "C-scenario".)

    On the other hand, Player 2 can always make sure that precisely one BkB_k-endpoint lies in V0V_0, therefore forcing Player 1 to either lose by picking a constant sequence {xn}n≥1\{x_n\}_{n\geq 1} or by triggering the C-scenario.

S000122Gustin's sequence spaceExample

Let ℤ+\mathbb{Z}^+ denote the set of positive integers, YY be the set of all finite sequences of positive integers of even length, and W={A⊆Y ∣ ∣A∣=2}W = \{A \subseteq Y\ |\ |A| = 2\}. Gustin's Sequence Space is the set X=Y∪(ℤ+×W)X = Y \cup (\mathbb{Z}^+ \times W) with topology defined as follows:

For any finite sequences α,β\alpha, \beta of arbitrary length, let αβ\alpha\beta be the sequence formed by adjoining β\beta to the end of α\alpha. Let α≥i∈ℤ\alpha \geq i \in \mathbb{Z} abbreviate a≥ia \geq i for every a∈αa \in \alpha. Let β⊇iα\beta \supseteq_i \alpha abbreviate that there exists a sequence of finite length γ≥i\gamma\geq i with β=αγ\beta = \alpha\gamma and Ui(α)={β∈Y ∣ β⊇iα}U_i(\alpha) = \{\beta \in Y\ |\ \beta \supseteq_i \alpha\}.

Let q:ℤ+×W→ℤ+q: \mathbb{Z}^+ \times W\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^+ be an injective function increasing on its first coordinate. (For example, fix a bijection pp from WW to the set of all positive primes, and define q:ℤ+×W→ℤ+q: \mathbb{Z}^+ \times W \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^+ by q(n,w)=[p(w)]nq(n,w) = [p(w)]^n.)

Define a topology on XX by letting neighborhoods of points α∈Y\alpha \in Y be sets of the form Ui(α)U_i(\alpha), and neighborhoods of points (n,w)=(n,{α,β})(n,w) = (n, \{\alpha, \beta\}) be sets of the form $V_i(n,w) = {(n,w)} \cup U_i\big(\alpha q(n,w)\big) \cup U_i\big(\beta q(n,w)\big) $.

Defined as counterexample #125 ("Gustin's Sequence Space") in Counterexamples in Topology.

S000125Knaster-Kuratowski fanExample

XX is a subspace of Euclidean Plane ℝ2\mathbb R^2 defined as follows. For any a∈[0,1]a \in [0,1], let L(a)L(a) be the closed line segment from (a,0)(a,0) to p=(12,12)p = (\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}). Let CC be the middle-thirds Cantor set in the unit interval, EE the set of endpoints of the removed intervals and F=C∖EF = C\setminus E. Define A={(x,y)∈L(c):c∈E,y∈ℚ}A = \{(x,y) \in L(c):c \in E, y \in \mathbb Q\} and B={(x,y)∈L(c):c∈F,y∉ℚ}B = \{(x,y) \in L(c):c \in F, y \not\in \mathbb Q\}. Then take X=A∪B⊆ℝ2X = A \cup B\subseteq\mathbb R^2 with the subspace topology.

The subspace X∖{p}X\setminus\{p\} obtained by removing the apex point is Punctured Knaster-Kuratowski fan.

Defined as counterexample #128 ("Cantor's Leaky Tent") in Counterexamples in Topology.

    Take some c∈Ec\in E. The projection map (x,y)↦y(x,y)\mapsto y maps L(c)L(c) homeomorphically onto [0,12][0,\frac12] and maps X∩L(c)X\cap L(c), which is a closed subset of XX, homeomorphically onto Y:=[0,12]∩ℚY:=[0,\frac12]\cap\mathbb Q.

    Now YY contains a closed set homeomorphic to Rational numbers ℚ\mathbb Q. For example, choose irrational numbers α,β\alpha,\beta with 0<α<β<120<\alpha<\beta<\frac12. The set Z:=(α,β)∩ℚZ:=(\alpha,\beta)\cap\mathbb Q is closed in YY. Since ZZ is countable, order-dense and without maximum or minimum element, it is order-isomorphic to ℚ\mathbb Q by Cantor's isomorphism theorem. And since ZZ is dense in (α,β)(\alpha,\beta), its order topology coincides with its induced subspace topology. So an order-isomorphism as above is a homeomorphism between ZZ and ℚ\mathbb Q.

    It follows that XX contains a closed set homeomorphic to Rational numbers ℚ\mathbb Q. Since Rational numbers ℚ\mathbb Q · Completely metrizable, neither is XX.

    Let YY be any subset of Cantor's Teepee containing more than one point. Our goal is to produce two sets AA and BB such that

    • AA and BB are separated open sets in the subspace topology induced by YY, and
    • Y=A∪BY = A \cup B.

    Since Cantor's Teepee is itself a subspace of the usual topology on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^2, we may revise these conditions to read

    • AA and BB are separated open sets in the usual topology on ℝ\mathbb{R}, and
    • Y⊆A∪BY \subseteq A \cup B.

    Now, suppose YY contains points p∈Xap \in X_a and q∈Xcq \in X_c with a≠ca \neq c (that is, YY witnesses more than one "strand" of the teepee). Choose any real number bb such that a<b<ca < b < c and bb lies in a deleted interval of the Cantor set. To obtain the separated open sets AA and BB, take any open set containing YY (or even the entire teepee) and "split" it along the line connecting (b,0)(b,0) and (1/2,1/2)(1/2,1/2) (see figure).

    !enter image description here

    Suppose instead that all points of YY belong to a single strand. The yy-coordinates of points belonging to this strand are either all rational or all irrational. In either case, we can easily separate the strand by passing our open sets through a point rr with yy-coordinate of the opposite type (see figure).

    !enter image description here

    Therefore every subset of Cantor's teepee with more than one point is disconnected, which is to say Cantor's teepee is totally disconnected.

    See item #2 for space #129 in Counterexamples in Topology.

S000128Miller's biconnected setExample

Let C⊂[0,1]C \subset [0,1] be the Cantor set. Let W=C×[0,1]⊂ℝ2W = C \times [0,1] \subset \mathbb{R}^2. Let KK be an indecomposable continuum such that K∩[0,1]2=WK \cap [0,1]^2 = W. Let Δ\Delta be a countable dense subset of KK (which exists, as KK is compact and metrizable). Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be the set of composants of KK, ℬ\mathcal{B} the set of continua which separate KK and 𝒟\mathcal{D} the set of subsets of Δ\Delta which are dense in some square S⊂[0,1]2S \subset [0,1]^2 which meets WW and has edges parallel to the xx- and yy- axes. Choose well orderings {Cα}\{C_\alpha\}, {Bα}\{B_\alpha\} and {Dα}\{D_\alpha\} of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, ℬ\mathcal{B} and 𝒟\mathcal{D} respectively for α<κ\alpha < \kappa where κ\kappa is the least ordinal with ∣κ∣=𝔠|\kappa| = \mathfrak{c}.

Inductively define for each α\alpha an Mα⊂KM_\alpha \subset K and simple closed curve JαJ_\alpha such that:

  1. Mα=pα∈Bα∩KM_\alpha = p_\alpha \in B_\alpha \cap K if Bα∩Δ=∅B_\alpha \cap \Delta = \emptyset
  2. Mα=∅M_\alpha = \emptyset if Bα∩Δ≠∅B_\alpha \cap \Delta \neq \emptyset
  3. For ordinals μ≠λ\mu \neq \lambda with Mμ,Mλ≠∅M_\mu, M_\lambda \neq \emptyset, MμM_\mu and MλM_\lambda are in different composants of KK
  4. JαJ_\alpha separates KK
  5. Jα∩Δ∖Dα=Jα∩M=∅J_\alpha \cap \Delta \setminus D_\alpha = J_\alpha \cap M = \emptyset where M=⋃α<κMαM = \bigcup_{\alpha < \kappa} M_\alpha

Let X=Δ∪M⊂ℝ2X = \Delta \cup M \subset \mathbb{R}^2 with the subspace topology.

Defined as counterexample #131 ("Miller's Biconnected Set") in Counterexamples in Topology.

    Trait evidence · P000055

    Define h:X→[0,+∞)h:X\to[0,+\infty) as h(x)=1∥x∥−1h(x)=\frac{1}{\|x\|}-1 and r:X→𝕊1r:X\to \mathbb S^1 as r(x):=1∥x∥xr(x):=\frac{1}{\|x\|}x. These are clearly continuous maps on XX (the topology is finer than Euclidean). Then consider a metric dd given by:

    • d(p,q)=∣h(p)−h(q)∣d(p,q)=|h(p)-h(q)|, if r(p)=r(q)r(p)=r(q);
    • d(p,q)=h(p)+h(q)+∥r(p)−r(q)∥d(p,q)=h(p)+h(q)+\|r(p)-r(q)\|, otherwise.

    Symmetry and reflexivity of dd is immediate. Triangle inequality requires consideration of few cases but is elementary as well.

    By continuity of rr and hh we obtain that convergence in the topology on XX implies convergence with respect to dd.

    Assume d(xn,x)→0d(x_n,x)\to 0 for some x∈Xx\in X and (xn)⊂X(x_n)\subset X. If h(x)>0h(x)>0, then clearly r(xn)=r(x)r(x_n)=r(x) for sufficiently large nn and ∥xn∥→∥x∥\|x_n\|\to \|x\|, implying convergence xn→xx_n \to x in XX. For h(x)=0h(x)=0, we have h(xn)→0h(x_n)\to 0 and r(xn)→r(x)=xr(x_n)\to r(x)=x in the Euclidean topology. But since xx inherits Euclidean Neighbourhoods we obtain convergence xn→xx_n\to x in this case as well. Hence dd is indeed a metric providing the topology on XX.

    To prove completeness of dd, observe that a Cauchy sequence (xn)⊂X(x_n)\subset X with respect to dd either satisfies h(xn)→0h(x_n)\to 0 or is eventually contained in one of the open radii. Since any radius (i.e. (0,1]⋅p(0,1]\cdot p with p∈𝕊1p\in \mathbb S^1) is isometric with [0,+∞)[0,+\infty), a Cauchy sequence contained therein has a limit. Now focus on the case h(xn)→0h(x_n)\to 0. Clearly, also (r(xn))(r(x_n)) has to be a Cauchy sequence. Since Euclidean metric on 𝕊1\mathbb S^1 is complete, there exists z:=lim⁡n→∞r(xn)z:=\lim_{n\to \infty} r(x_n). Since also h(xn)→0h(x_n)\to 0, we obtain d(xn,z)→0d(x_n,z)\to 0, which ends the proof.

S000131Sequential fan with ω\omega-many spinesExample

The space X=SωX=S_\omega is obtained from the disjoint union of a countably infinite number of convergent sequences (Fort space on a countably infinite set) by identifying all the limit points to a single point ∞\infty.

So X=(ω×ω)∪{∞}X=(\omega\times\omega)\cup\{\infty\} as sets, with all the points of ω×ω\omega\times\omega isolated and neighborhoods of ∞\infty being the sets omitting finitely many points from each of the columns of ω×ω\omega\times\omega. Basic open neighborhoods of ∞\infty are given by the sets Uf={∞}∪{(m,n)∈ω×ω:n≥f(m)}U_f=\{\infty\}\cup\{(m,n)\in\omega\times\omega:n\ge f(m)\} for some arbitrary function f:ω→ωf:\omega\to\omega.

See also https://dantopology.wordpress.com/2015/07/01/a-note-on-products-of-sequential-fans for useful information.

Compare with the coarser topology of Metric fan with ω\omega-many spines.

S000132Duncan's spaceExample

Let AA be the set of all strictly increasing, infinite sequences of positive integers. For any x∈Ax\in A, define N(n,x)N(n,x) as the number of elements of xx less than nn. Let δ(x)=lim⁡n→∞N(n,x)n\delta (x) =\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{N(n,x)}{n}. Let XX be the subset of AA containing precisely the sequences xx for which δ(x)\delta(x) exists. Now for any x,y∈Xx,y\in X define k(x,y)k(x,y) to be the smallest index ii such that xi≠yix_i\neq y_i. We define a metric d(x,y)d(x,y) on XX as $$d(x,y)=\frac{1}{k(x,y)}+|\delta (x) - \delta (y)| \text{ with } d(x,x)=0.$$ Duncan's Space is the topology on XX induced by this metric.

Defined as counterexample #136 ("Duncan's Space") in Counterexamples in Topology.

S000133Real line with post office metricExample

A space XX with a particular point pp satisfying:

  • Each point x≠px\ne p is isolated.
  • The point pp has a countable neighborhood base {Vn:n<ω}\{V_n:n<\omega\} such that V0=XV_0=X, Vn+1⊆VnV_{n+1}\subseteq V_n and ∣Vn∖Vn+1∣=∣ℝ∣|V_n\setminus V_{n+1}|=|\mathbb R| for each n, and ⋂n<ωVn={p}\bigcap_{n<\omega}V_n=\{p\}.

These conditions uniquely determine the space XX up to homeomorphism, as shown in Name for topology generated by the standard open sets of reals and every point that isn't zero..

Here are a few examples of spaces satisfying the conditions (see mathse 4834226).

  • The space X=ℝX=\mathbb{R} with p=0p=0. The basic open neighborhoods of 00 are the Euclidean open intervals around 00.

  • The post office metric space defined as counterexample #139 ("The Post Office Metric") in Counterexamples in Topology, where X=ℝnX=\mathbb R^n with n≥1n\ge 1 and pp is the origin. The post office metric dd on ℝn\mathbb R^n is defined by:

d(x,y)={0if x=y,∥x∥+∥y∥otherwise.d(x,y) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } x=y, \\ \|x\| + \|y\| & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}

S000134Radial metric on the planeExample

If ded_e is the usual Euclidean metric on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^2, the radial metric rr is defined by:

r(x,y)={de(x,y),x and y are collinear with 0⃗de(x,0⃗)+de(y,0⃗),otherwise.r(x,y) = \begin{cases} d_e(x,y), & x \text{ and } y \text{ are collinear with } \vec 0\\ d_e(x,\vec 0) + d_e(y,\vec 0), & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}

Defined as counterexample #140 ("The Radial Metric") in Counterexamples in Topology.

  • Locally path connected
    Trait evidence · P000042

    Every open half line emanating from the origin is isometric to Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R and Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R · Locally path connected.

  • Completely metrizable
    Trait evidence · P000055

    The metric rr is complete. Every line passing through the origin is isometric to Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R, hence a Cauchy sequence eventually contained in such a line has a limit by completeness of the Euclidean metric.

    Assume (xn)(x_n) is a Cauchy sequence not contained in a line, i.e. for every nn there exists n′>nn'>n such that xnx_n and xn′x_{n'} are not collinear with 0⃗\vec 0. Then r(xn,xn′)=de(xn,0⃗)+de(xn′,0⃗)≥r(xn,0⃗)r(x_n,x_{n'}) = d_e(x_n,\vec 0)+d_e(x_{n'},\vec 0)\geq r(x_n,\vec 0). The assumption r(xn,xm)→0r(x_n,x_m)\to 0 (for n,m→∞n,m\to \infty) implies r(xn,0⃗)→0r(x_n,\vec 0)\to 0, hence xn→0⃗x_n\to\vec 0.

    Trait evidence · P000205

    The space is Connected.

S000135Radial interval topology on ℝ2\mathbb R^2Example

The radial interval topology on the plane X=ℝ2X=\mathbb{R}^2 is generated by the basis consisting of open intervals disjoint from the origin on lines passing through the origin, along with sets of the form ⋃{Iθ:0≤θ<π}\bigcup\{I_\theta : 0 \leq \theta < \pi\} where IθI_\theta is an open interval about the origin on the line with slope tan⁡θ\tan\theta.

This space is homeomorphic to the quotient of the disjoint union of continuum many copies of Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R with the points 00 of all of the copies identified to a single point.

Defined as counterexample #141 ("Radial Interval Topology") in Counterexamples in Topology.

S000138Rudin's Dowker spaceExample

Rudin's Dowker space XX is the subset of the product ∏n<ω(ωn+1+1)\prod_{n<\omega}(\omega_{n+1}+1) with the box topology consisting of all functions ff such that, for some i<ωi<\omega, we have ω<cf(f(n))<ωi\omega< \mathrm{cf}(f(n))<\omega_i for all n∈ωn\in\omega. By cf(λ)\mathrm{cf}(\lambda) we denote the cofinality of λ\lambda (see Cofinality on Wikipedia).

See A normal space X for which X×I is not normal (M.E. Rudin) and section 3.2(i) of Dowker spaces (M.E. Rudin).

S000139Countable bouquet of circlesExample

Let X=ℝ/ℤX=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z to be the quotient of ℝ\mathbb R (with its Euclidean topology) obtained by identifying all the points of ℤ\mathbb Z to a single point ∞\infty.

Alternatively, this space can be characterized as the wedge sum (see Wedge sum on Wikipedia) of countably-many circles, also known as a bouquet of countably many circles.

Not to be confused with Infinite earring, which has a coarser topology.

S000140ℝ\mathbb{R} extended by a point with co-countable open neighborhoodsExample

Let X=ℝ∪{∞}X=\mathbb R\cup \{\infty\}. Let ℝ\mathbb R be open in XX and have the topology of Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R, and let open neighborhoods of ∞\infty be given by sets of the form U∪{∞}U\cup\{\infty\}, where U⊆ℝU\subseteq \mathbb R is co-countable and open in the Euclidean topology.

Constructed in Answer to 'Radial/pseudoradial implies Fréchet-Urysohn/sequential for locally countable spaces' as an example of a space that is Pseudoradial and Countably tight, yet fails to be Sequential, yielding a counterexample to a natural analogue of (Countably tight ∧ Radial) ⇒ Fréchet Urysohn. Elaborated on in What are the compactness properties of $\mathbb R$, extended by a point with co-countable open neighborhoods?.

S000142Erdős spaceExample

The subspace XX of ℓ2\ell^2 consisting of those sequences x=(xi)ix=(x_i)_i with all xi∈ℚx_i\in\mathbb Q.

The space ℓ2\ell^2 is the Banach space of sequences of real numbers x=(xi)ix=(x_i)_i with ∑ixi2<∞\sum_i x_i^2<\infty, equipped with the norm ∥x∥2=(∑ixi2)1/2\|x\|_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2} and corresponding distance and topology.

The space ℓ2\ell^2 is topologically homeomorphic to Countable product of reals ℝω\mathbb R^\omega; but note the space XX is not homeomorphic to the subspace Countable product of rationals ℚω\mathbb Q^\omega of ℝω\mathbb R^\omega.

    The idea is to consider the map φ:X→ℚω×ℝ\varphi:X\to\mathbb Q^\omega\times\mathbb R defined by φ(x)=(x,∥x∥)\varphi(x)=(x,\|x\|), where ℚω\mathbb Q^\omega in the codomain has the product topology. This follows from the fact that both domain and codomain are metric spaces, and a sequence (xn)n(x_n)_n of points in the Hilbert space ℓ2\ell^2 converges to the point x∈ℓ2x\in\ell^2 iff xnx_n converges componentwise to xx and ∥xn∥→∥x∥\|x_n\|\to\|x\| (see for example mathse 1326803 and mathse 214248). S000143Butterfly spaceExample

The space X=ℝ×[0,∞)X=\mathbb R\times [0,\infty) is the closed upper half-plane topologized as follows. Points above the xx-axis have their usual Euclidean neighborhoods. A local base for a point p=⟨px,0⟩p=\langle p_x,0\rangle on the xx-axis is formed by the "butterfly neighborhoods" Nε(p)N_\varepsilon(p) for ε>0\varepsilon>0, where Nε(p)N_\varepsilon(p) consists of pp together with all points q=⟨qx,qy⟩q=\langle q_x,q_y\rangle at distance less than ε\varepsilon from pp and lying underneath the union of the two rays in XX that emanate from pp and have slopes ε\varepsilon and −ε-\varepsilon. In formula, $$N_\varepsilon(p)={p} \cup {q\in X:|q-p|<\varepsilon\text{ and }q_y<\varepsilon|q_x-p_x|}.$$

Defined as Example 12.1 in $\aleph_0$-spaces (E. Michael) (https://www.jstor.org/stable/24901448).

Exercise 3.1.I in General Topology (Engelking, 1989) defines a very similar space of the same name, with a slightly different topology but essentially the same properties.

Sources cited by Pi-Base

  • $\aleph_0$-spaces (E. Michael)
  • General Topology (Engelking, 1989)

S000144Diamond poset 2×22\times 2 with Alexandrov topologyExample

Let P=({0,a,b,1},≤)P=(\{0,a,b,1\},\le) be the four-element poset with 00 as minimum element, 11 as maximum element, and the remaining elements aa and bb incomparable. This poset is order-isomorphic to the Boolean algebra with four elements. The space XX is PP with the corresponding Alexandrov topology, whose open sets are the upper sets for ≤\le.

The name "diamond poset" is used for example in Diamond-free families (Griggs, Li & Lu).

S000145Free ultrafilter topology on ω\omegaExample

The space XX is the set ω\omega with topology τ=𝒰∪{∅}\tau=\mathscr U\cup\{\emptyset\}, where 𝒰\mathscr U is a free ultrafilter on ω\omega.

The space is described for example in Examples of connected door spaces and as item (3) in Theorem 1 of Connected door spaces and topological solutions of equations (Wu, Wang, Zhang).

Not to be confused with Single ultrafilter subspace of βω\beta\omega.

Note: The topology on XX depends on the choice of ultrafilter. There are 2𝔠2^{\mathfrak c} homeomorphism classes of such spaces (see for example Answer to "Are there uncountably many non homeomorphic ways to topologize a countably infinite set?"). However, the properties currently tracked in π-Base for this space do not depend on that choice.

  • Biconnected
    Trait evidence · P000044

    Let YY be a Connected subset of XX with at least two points. If YY is closed in XX, by the property of ultrafilters all subsets of YY are closed, thus YY is Discrete, which is not possible. This implies that YY is open, that is, every Connected subset of XX must be open.

    Now, because XX is Connected, XX cannot be partitioned into two nonempty open subsets. We conclude that XX cannot be partitioned into two Connected subsets, each with at least two points.

S000147(CH) A Luzin subset of the reals (The special Lusin set LL)Example

An uncountable subset of the reals such that its intersection with every nowhere dense subset of the reals (equivalently, every meager subset of the reals) is countable. For background information, see the article Luzin spaces (K. Kunen), available at the Topology Proceedings webpage.

Note that the construction of such a set requires additional axioms beyond ZFCZFC.

Here we use the CHCH construction from Lemma 2.6 of The combinatorics of open covers II (Just et al) in order to guarantee the failure of ω\omega-Rothberger.

  • Luzin spaces (K. Kunen)
  • The combinatorics of open covers II (Just et al)

S000149Two-sided long lineExample

This space XX is constructed from Long ray with a mirror copy extending in the other direction.

Let LL denote the Long ray ω1×[0,1)\omega_1\times[0,1) with the lexicographic order and let L∗L^\ast be a copy of LL with the reverse order. As an ordered set, XX is obtained from L∗L^\ast followed by LL with max⁡(L∗)\max(L^\ast) and min⁡(L)\min(L) identified. It is given the corresponding order topology.

S000150Right "closed-ray" topology on [0,1]∩ℚ[0,1]\cap\mathbb QExample

The set X=[0,1]∩ℚX=[0,1]\cap\mathbb Q with its order induced from ℝ\mathbb R, and the topology generated by a base of open sets consisting of the intervals [x,→)[x,\rightarrow) for x∈Xx\in X.

The open sets are exactly the upward-closed sets in the ordered set (X,≤)(X,\le). That includes "closed rays" [x,→)[x,\rightarrow) and "open rays" (x,→)(x,\rightarrow) for x∈Xx\in X, as well as sets of the form (θ,1]∩ℚ(\theta,1]\cap\mathbb Q for an irrational θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1).

The closed sets are the downward-closed sets in (X,≤)(X,\le).

Compare with the coarser topology of Right "open-ray" topology on [0,1]∩ℚ[0,1]\cap\mathbb Q.

S000152Poset {−1,0a,0b}∪{1/n}n=1∞\{-1,0_a,0_b\}\cup\{1/n\}_{n=1}^\infty with Alexandrov topologyExample

Consider the set {1/n}n=1∞\{1/n\}_{n=1}^\infty with its usual order. Let

X={−1,0a,0b}∪{1/n}n=1∞\quad X=\{-1,0_a,0_b\}\cup\{1/n\}_{n=1}^\infty

where either of the zeros is smaller than all 1/n1/n, the two zeros are incomparable, and −1-1 is smaller than everything else. Then equip XX with the Alexandrov topology associated to the partial order defined above; that is, the open sets are the upper sets for ≤\le.

S000153Open long rayExample

The space obtained by taking Y=ω1×[0,1)Y=\omega_1 \times [0,1) with its lexicographic order topology (Long ray) and removing the first element ⟨0,0⟩\langle 0,0 \rangle.

S000154Fort space on the real numbersExample

Let X=ℝ∪{∞}X=\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}. Every point of ℝ\mathbb R is isolated and the open neighborhoods of the point ∞\infty are the cofinite subsets of XX containing that point.

This space is the one-point compactification of an uncountable discrete space (compare with Fortissimo space on ℝ\mathbb R and Fort space on a countably infinite set).

Defined as counterexample #24 ("Uncountable Fort Space") in Counterexamples in Topology.

    Suppose that XX is cozero complemented and let U⊆ℝU\subseteq \mathbb{R} be any countably infinite set. Then UU is an open FσF_\sigma-set, so it follows that UU is a cozero set. Find a cozero set VV disjoint from UU such that U∪VU\cup V is dense in XX. Since X∖VX\setminus V is infinite we have ∞∉V\infty\notin V. Since VV is a cozero set, write V=⋃n=1∞FnV = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty F_n where FnF_n are closed. Then ∞∉Fn\infty\notin F_n so FnF_n is finite. It follows that VV is countable. But then X=U∪V‾=U∪V∪{∞}X = \overline{U\cup V} = U\cup V\cup \{\infty\} is countable, contradiction.

S000155Fortissimo space of size ℵ1\aleph_1Example

Let XX be a set of cardinality ℵ1\aleph_1 with a distinguished point p∈Xp\in X. Every point not equal to pp is isolated and the open neighborhoods of pp are the cocountable subsets of XX containing that point.

This space is the one-point Lindelöfication of a discrete space of size ℵ1\aleph_1.

If (CH) 2ℵ0=ℵ12^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_1 holds, this space is homeomorphic to Fortissimo space on ℝ\mathbb R. Compare also with Fortissimo space of size ℵ2\aleph_2.

For a general XX with unspecified uncountable cardinality, see counterexample #25 ("Fortissimo Space") in Counterexamples in Topology.

In theorem 5.6 it's shown that 𝒜(κ)\mathcal{A}(\kappa) implies that L(κ)L(\kappa) is robustly Menger, where L(κ)L(\kappa) is the one-point Lindelöfication of discrete space of size κ\kappa. In this case L(ω1)L(\omega_1) is Fortissimo space of size ℵ1\aleph_1. From theorem 5.5 it follows that robustly Menger implies 2-Markov Menger, so S000155 · P000072.

S000156Arens spaceExample

Let X=ω∪{∞}X=\omega\cup\{\infty\} be the one-point compactification of a countable discrete space. Arens space S2S_2 is the minimal topology on (X×ω)∪{∞′}(X\times\omega)\cup\{\infty'\} where ({∞}×ω)∪{∞′}(\{\infty\}\times\omega)\cup\{\infty'\} is homeomorphic to XX.

This space was originally defined by Richard Arens in mr 0037500.

The subspace (ω×ω)∪{∞′}(\omega\times\omega)\cup\{\infty'\} of the Arens space is homeomorphic to Arens-Fort Space, as mentioned in Examples 2.10 and 3.10 of Mapping theorems on countable tightness and a question of F. Siwiec (Lin & Zhang).

S000157Fortissimo space of size ℵ2\aleph_2Example

Let XX be a set of cardinality ℵ2\aleph_2 with a distinguished point p∈Xp\in X. Every point not equal to pp is isolated and the open neighborhoods of pp are the cocountable subsets of XX containing that point.

This space is the one-point Lindelöfication of a discrete space of size ℵ2\aleph_2.

If 2ℵ0=ℵ22^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2 holds, this space is homeomorphic to Fortissimo space on ℝ\mathbb R. Compare also with Fortissimo space of size ℵ1\aleph_1.

For a general XX with unspecified uncountable cardinality, see counterexample #25 ("Fortissimo Space") in Counterexamples in Topology.

S000168Real projective plane ℝP2\mathbb RP^2Example

The quotient of Sphere S2S^2 which identifies its antipodal points.

This space is homeomorphic to:

  • (ℝ3∖{0})/∼\left( \mathbb R^3 \setminus \{0\} \right) / \sim, where x∼yx \sim y if and only if x=cyx = c y for some nonzero real number cc.
  • The space of 11-dimensional subspaces of the real vector space ℝ3\mathbb{R}^3, P(ℝ3)P(\mathbb{R}^3), with the quotient topology induced by the map ℝ3∖{0}→P(ℝ3)\mathbb R^3 \setminus \{0\} \to P(\mathbb{R}^3) which sends a vector to its span.
  • The quotient of [−1,1]2\left[ -1, 1 \right]^2 identifying (t,1)(t, 1) with (−t,−1)(-t, -1) and identifying (1,t)(1, t) with (−1,−t)(-1, -t), for each tt.

Defined in Example 3.51 and Proposition 6.2 of Introduction to topological manifolds (Lee).

S000169Sphere S2S^2Example

The subspace {x∈ℝ3:∥x∥=1}\{x \in \mathbb{R}^3: \|x\| = 1\} of the Euclidean space ℝ3\mathbb{R}^3 consisting of points with distance 1 from the origin.

This space is homeomorphic to:

  • The one-point compactification of Euclidean Plane ℝ2\mathbb R^2,
  • The suspension of Circle S1S^1, i.e., the quotient of S1×[0,1]S^1 \times [0,1] where S1×{0}S^1 \times \{0\} is identified to a single point and S1×{1}S^1 \times \{1\} is identified to a single point.
